title: There's No Better Feeling Than Knowing You're Getting Better
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Profiling longtime UC Berkeley rugby coach Jack Clark, this article explores what drives sustained motivation in top performers: not achievement alone, but the felt experience of visible progress. Clark's method centers on amplifying players' strengths in private conversations before challenging them with high expectations and tough feedback. The piece argues this sequencing matters, since confidence built from magnified strengths gives people the resilience to absorb criticism without feeling diminished. The takeaway for leaders is that durable high performance is built by making growth visible and celebrated, not just by demanding results.
points: Jack Clark's 40-year record at Cal rugby stems from a philosophy that people are motivated most by visible progress, not just outcomes.
He privately magnifies players' strengths in detail before pushing them harder, building a foundation of confidence first.
Marking clear improvement earns Clark the credibility to demand more from his players.
This 'blowing up' of strengths acts as armor that lets players absorb intense feedback without self-doubt.
The broader lesson: leaders who make improvement visible build cultures where people chase excellence for its own sake.
quotes: Clark believes that one thing motivates high performers more than anything else— a leader who invests in making people better.
In Clark’s view, there is no better feeling in the world than knowing you are making progress and getting better.
Every time he points out that a player has made marked improvement, he earns their implicit permission to demand even more.
It is this balance of magnified strengths and intense feedback that propels them forward, allowing continuous progress and improvement.
The most effective path to high performance runs through growth, not just achievement.
